social.name: Pana Social
social.headline:
Social Media
That Is Private
and Local
social.lede: A social network for South Florida, owned by the people in it. Private by default, local on purpose, and built to connect panas who already work together.

pillars.statement: Pana Social is designed for Local Life.

one.name: Local
one.body: Everyone here is in Broward, Miami-Dade or Palm Beach — the makers and shops you can actually walk to. Not a global feed that buries the bakery down the street.

two.name: Private
two.body: No ad auction, no tracking pixels, no profile of you built and sold on. Nobody here measures your attention, because nobody here is selling it.

three.name: Connected
three.body: The panas you follow are the same ones in the directory and behind the tables at events. A follow here can turn into a booking, a collab or a shared stall.

tour.title: How It Works
tour.lede: Five screens, one neighborhood. Each one is a different way back to the same people.

feed.name: The Feed
feed.title: Your block, in the order it happened
feed.body: Posts from panas across Broward, Miami-Dade and Palm Beach, newest first — no ranking deciding which neighbor you hear from. The canal at 6am, the pop-up on Saturday, the studio with a free table going spare. Things close enough to actually go to.

groups.name: Groups
groups.title: A room for every corner of the scene
groups.body: A neighborhood, a craft, a project, a mutual aid run. Groups are where a loose follow turns into people who plan something together — and they stay small enough that showing up still counts for something.

events.name: Events
events.title: Where a post becomes a door you walk through
events.body: Markets, mixers, workshops and shows, posted by the panas actually running them and carrying a real going count. The whole point of a local feed is that you can close it and be there in twenty minutes.

profiles.name: Pana Profiles
profiles.title: The person behind the work
profiles.body: A profile here is the same pana you find in the directory — the shop, the craft, the portfolio and the posts in one place. You meet somebody in the feed and you can book them by the end of the afternoon.

stories.name: Stories
stories.title: Today, before it disappears
stories.body: Tap a pana's face and watch their day go by — the stall going up, the line at the window, the sky over the canal. Stories last twenty-four hours and then they're gone, which is exactly the point: an invitation to today, not a permanent record to perform for.

one.title: No algorithm
one.body: Newest first, every time. Nothing is promoted, buried or reordered to keep you scrolling, because nobody here earns anything from how long you stay.

two.title: No ad profile
two.body: No tracking pixels, no data brokers, no version of you assembled and sold on. Your attention is not the product, so it is not being measured.

three.title: An address that travels
three.body: Your handle is @you@panamia.club and it speaks ActivityPub, so a post here reaches Mastodon too — and if you ever leave, your panas come with you.

closing.lede: Every other timeline you read belongs to someone whose business is selling your attention back to you. This one belongs to the people in it.

directory.name: Directory
directory.headline:
Find Your
People
directory.lede: South Florida's living archive of the creatives, entrepreneurs and small businesses who make this place what it is — written by them, not scraped from somewhere else.

problem.statement: The top of the page is for sale.

one.title: The results are bought
one.body: Search “near me” and the first screen belongs to whoever has an ad budget. Proximity is a filter there, never the ranking.

two.title: Someone else wrote your page
two.body: A review site decides what your business is, in a stranger’s words, under a star rating you never agreed to.

three.title: The smallest ones aren't there at all
three.body: No storefront, no sign, no ad spend — a kitchen, a booth, a spare room. Invisible to a map that only knows addresses.

steps.title: How It Works
steps.lede: Three things happen before a name reaches you, and there is a person involved in every one of them.

one.title: Panas write themselves in
one.body: Your name, five words, your tags, your neighborhood. You describe what you do — nobody summarizes you.

two.title: A human approves it
two.body: Every submission is read before it goes live, and the rule is short: you live or work in Broward, Miami-Dade or Palm Beach.

three.title: Then you can actually find it
three.body: Search by keyword, category, county or distance — and it turns up Café, Bodegón and Lucía whether or not you typed the accent.

one.title: Somebody to call
one.body: Every result is a person or a shop with a name, a neighborhood and a way to reach them. Not a lead form.

two.title: Visible without a budget
two.body: Placement isn't for sale here. A one-person operation sits in the same list as everybody else.

three.title: A record of who was here
three.body: The directory is an archive as much as a search box — South Florida’s small operators, in their own words, kept year after year.

closing.lede: The directory exists so that the next time you need something, the answer is a neighbor with a name rather than whoever paid the most for the top of the page.

events.name: Events
events.headline:
Show Up
Somewhere
events.lede: Markets, workshops, art builds and long dinners across South Florida — co-hosted with the people already doing the work.

one.title: It's announced, then it's gone
one.body: The night lives in a story that deletes itself in twenty-four hours. Miss that day and, as far as you know, it never happened.

two.title: The flyer leaves out the part you need
two.body: A date and no address, or an address and no hour. Never whether there is still room for you when you get there.

three.title: You find out on Monday
three.body: Everyone who went heard about it in a group chat you are not in. You see it afterwards, in somebody else’s photos.

steps.title: How It Works
steps.lede: Three things, and the first one is as open to you as it is to anybody else.

one.title: A pana puts it up
one.body: Any pana can post an event — the date, the venue, and what it actually is. You do not need a room of your own or a budget to start.

two.title: You say you're coming
two.body: RSVP without an account. A link lands in your email, you open it, and you are counted — going, maybe, or can’t make it.

three.title: It lands in your calendar
three.body: One tap puts it in whatever calendar you already live by, so showing up stops depending on you remembering.

one.title: Nights worth staying at
one.body: Markets, workshops, art builds and long dinners. Gatherings built for talking to people rather than for handing out cards.

two.title: Going means going
two.body: RSVPs stop at the room's real limit — the venue's fire capacity, not somebody's guess — so a confirmed spot is an actual spot.

three.title: Near you, or worth the drive
three.body: Broward, Miami-Dade and Palm Beach on one calendar. What is happening down the street this week, or the one worth an hour up the coast.

closing.lede: A directory tells you who is out there. An event is where you actually meet them. Come to one, then host the next.

vizion.name: PanaVizión
vizion.headline:
Local, On
The Record
vizion.lede: A video series with the people building South Florida's local economy — two panas at a time, talking to each other rather than into a microphone.

one.title: The story arrives from out of town
one.body: National coverage of South Florida is beaches, money and nightlife. The people who actually hold the place together are the extras in it.

two.title: You get a blurb, not a conversation
two.body: Local press covers the opening and the closing. The years in between — which are the actual work — go unrecorded.

three.title: And then the link rots
three.body: A feature runs, traffic spikes for a day, and it is gone. Nothing is left that somebody could still find in five years.

steps.title: How It Works
steps.lede: Three decisions about how it gets recorded, and not one of them is the decision a news segment would make.

one.title: Two panas, one room
one.body: Each episode pairs two local makers and lets them talk to each other — a tattoo artist with a musician, a ceramicist with a farmer. The interview is between them. We just roll.

two.title: At whatever length it takes
two.body: No four-minute segment, no soundbite. The conversation runs until it is finished, because the setbacks are the part that takes a while to say out loud.

three.title: And it stays up
three.body: Every episode is published and left there — watchable, searchable and linkable long after the week it went out.

one.title: Names you already walk past
one.body: Episodes with the people behind Easy Peasy Tattoos, Earth Pallas, Folktale San Pedro, Dear Eleanor and Golden Flora — places you could visit this week.

two.title: An archive, not a feed
two.body: Everything stays findable long after the week it aired, because the point of it is the record rather than the release.

three.title: Your turn on the record
three.body: Panas get pitched, featured and interviewed. If you are doing the work here, it belongs in the archive in your own words.

closing.lede: Who gets recorded is who gets remembered. PanaVizión exists so that the people holding South Florida together are in the archive, not just in the traffic.

ink.name: Pana Ink Press
ink.headline:
Words You
Can Hand Over
ink.lede: Zines, pamphlets and printed matter that carry the local movement off the screen and into somebody’s hands.

problem.statement: Everything else we make needs a battery.

one.title: A link needs a reason to be opened
one.body: You can send somebody the directory. Whether they open it is a separate question, and most of the time the answer is later.

two.title: A feed does not reach everyone
two.body: Plenty of the people who make this place run are on no platform we publish to. Reaching them through a feed means not reaching them.

three.title: Platforms change their minds
three.body: Anything we host can be throttled, blocked or switched off by somebody else. Paper cannot be deprecated.

steps.title: How It Works
steps.lede: Three things, and it starts with what is already written.

one.title: We print what already exists
one.body: The dispatches — the long reads about panas building this economy — get written and published first. The press begins by putting them on paper.

two.title: Made with local artists
two.body: Short runs designed alongside panas who draw, letter and lay out. A zine is a collaboration, and the people making it are in the directory.

three.title: Handed over, not sold
three.body: Stacks go to markets, shops and events to be given away. There is no subscriber list, because the whole point is that it travels without one.

one.title: Something to hand over
one.body: A zine you can put in someone's hands at a market. No link to send, no app to install, no reason for them to say later.

two.title: The dispatches
two.body: Long reads from the people building South Florida's local economy — published now, and the raw material for what gets printed first.

three.title: Print as infrastructure
three.body: Paper keeps working when a platform changes its mind. That is the whole argument for a community owning a press of its own.

closing.lede: A zine handed to someone at a market reaches further than a post does, and it is still there next year. The press is how the movement travels off the screen.

getInvolved.name: Get Involved
getInvolved.headline:
Start Where
You Are
getInvolved.lede: Pana MIA is built by the people in it. There is a way in at every size, and the first one costs nothing but showing up.

problem.statement: Wanting to help is not the hard part.

one.title: There is rarely a door
one.body: Most groups doing good work here have no obvious way to join them. You find out after it happened, from somebody who was already inside.

two.title: The ask is always money
two.body: Plenty of people have an hour, a van, a storefront or a trade and nowhere to offer it, because the only button on the page says donate.

three.title: You never learn if it mattered
three.body: Help that disappears into an organization is hard to repeat. People come back when they can see what their hour turned into.

steps.title: Ways In
steps.lede: Three of them, in order of how much they ask.

one.title: Show up to something
one.body: Come to a market, a workshop or a meetup. No form, no membership, no money — the events are open, and this is how most panas started.

two.title: Become a pana
two.body: Fill out the sign-up form and get a profile in the directory. It takes a few minutes, a person reads it, and we email you when you are live.

three.title: Run a pod
three.body: Community Connectors are neighborhood pods across Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach running their own projects. Three tiers, and everybody starts at the first.

one.title: Neighbors who can find you
one.body: A profile your community can search by name, trade or neighborhood — and one more local name standing behind the club.

two.title: People nearby already doing it
two.body: A pod in your own county working on the street you live on, instead of a volunteer list two cities away.

three.title: Something that stays yours
three.body: Members and donations pay for the directory, the feed and the events. That is the reason none of it has to sell your attention.

closing.lede: Pana MIA was started so that anyone with an idea for making South Florida better had somewhere to bring it. Bring yours.

connectors.name: Pana Connectors
connectors.headline:
Organize Where
You Already Are
connectors.lede: Community Connectors are the volunteers who keep Pana MIA running — neighborhood pods across Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach, each one building the South Florida they actually want to live in.

one.title: Everyone starts from scratch
one.body: The zine, the free market, the food share — somebody already worked out how to run each one, and wrote none of it down. The next person begins at zero.

two.title: Nobody can see the whole
two.body: Dozens of people are organizing across three counties right now. Because none of it is counted together, it reads to a funder as scattered effort rather than as a movement.

three.title: Burnout does the sorting
three.body: With no tiers and no handover, the only way to stay involved is to do everything. So the people who care most are the ones who leave first.

steps.title: How It Works
steps.lede: Choose a major and a minor house, join a pod, start at the first tier. Everybody starts at the first tier.

one.title: Choose your two houses
one.body: Choose two different houses from the four: a major for your primary focus and a minor for your secondary focus. Both are required and reflect what you already like doing, not assignments or limits on where you can help.

two.title: Join your pod
two.body: Pods are geographic — Miami-Dade, Broward, Palm Beach. A pod is a third space: somewhere to bring a project, argue it out, and be held to it. Each one runs its own Signal chat.

three.title: Start at Tier One
three.body: Tiers are about how much you are taking on, not how good you are. One assists the builders, two builds, three supports other builders and brings what the pod learned back to everyone else.

one.title: A pod on your own block
one.body: Panas in your county working on the street you live on — not a volunteer list two cities away that emails you when something needs carrying.

two.title: Work that counts for something
two.body: Pods report what they did back to roots, so a hundred small actions can be shown as one body of work. That is what turns into funding, venues and a say in the story being told about South Florida.

three.title: A library to build from
three.body: PITbooks — Praxis Informed Theory books — are living how-tos for the things we already know how to do. Hydration stations, food shares, zine displays, free markets. You start from the last person's ending.

closing.statement: History is not transformed by packed squares.
closing.lede: It is transformed by groups and collectives that know and recognize one another, below and to the left, and build another world. That is the whole job. Come do it with us.
